latin.106:
CAPUT X.

Imputationem primi Adae peccati actualis antecedentem seu immediatam nullis rationibus astrui posse.

Putasne, Lector, hanc imputationem, cum absit a Scriptura, rationibus posse astrui? Audiamus tamen, si quae afferuntur, rationes. Persuasum enim est nobis perpetuo cum Scriptura rectam consentire rationem. Agnosco, Quae Deus Adamo largitus erat, non ipsi soli, sed etiam toti posteritati ipsius fuisse data; ac proinde nos in ipsius persona omnibus illis bonis spoliatos in omnem hanc miseriam & maledictionem incidisse. Quid inde pro illa imputatione rationis elici potest? Erant-ne posteris omnibus imputanda, quae Deus Adamo largitus fuerat bona? Aut est-ne imputanda nobis illorum omnium bonorum Adamo conveniens spoliatio? Utinam haec spoliatio nobis nonnisi imputative conveniret!
latin.107: Qui, inquit, propter parentum crimen actuale aliquod, iis beneficiis privantur, quae parentes illi & pro se & pro liberis suis acceperant; illi paterni criminis poenas luunt, atque adeo paternum crimen illis imputatur. Atqui posteri omnes Adami propter primam illam ejus inobedientiam qua se polluit, privantur iis beneficiis, quae Adamus pro se & pro posteris suis acceperat, nimirum, justitia & rectitudine naturali. Ergo posteri omnes naturales Adami paterni criminis poenas luunt, adeoque paternum illis crimen imputatur. Quid si hanc conclusionem concedam? Paternum enim crimen vel vitium haereditarium intelligitur, vel causa illius vitii, actualis inobedientia Adami. Si prius, imputatur, & quidem immediate. Si posterius, imputatur id quoque, sed mediante inhaerente vitio. Luimus poenas proxime peccati nostri in nos propagati, remote vero peccati ab Adamo olim admissi. Quod si dicat aliquis, nos omnes transgressioni Adae nasci obnoxios, immediate, hoc est, non propter aliquod vitium, aut culpam, aut depravationem, quam in nobis habeamus, is meminerit sic fuisse Pighii errorem a Petro Martyre explicatum: atque his argumentis in primis confutatum: quae considera, Lector, si placet, annon pugnent cum D. G. sententia & argumentis.
latin.108: Verum, inquit, contra hanc sententiam in primis illud facit, quod jam bis diximus: videlicet, infantes mori. Mors enim nihil juris habet ubi non est peccatum. Nisi dicere velimus Deum punire innocentem. Confirmatur autem haec ratio ex argumento Pauli, quo probavit, peccatum fuisse ante Legem. Quia mors, inquit, regnavit ab Adamo usque ad Mosen. Atqui juxta Pighii sententiam haec ratio hebetissima videri possit. Diceret enim quispiam, etsi illi mortui fuerint, tamen ex eo non sequitur, illos habuisse peccatum. Mors enim illis contigit propter Adamum, ob cujus peccatum redditi sint mortales. Vides, Lector, & peccatum intelligi, non actuale Adami, ut vult D. Garissolius, sed habituale nostrum; & pro causa Pighii ejus argumenta militare adversus nostros. Quod ut fiat manifestius, subjungam aliud argumentum Martyris. Postremo, inquit, habemus a Paulo per inobedientiam unius hominis multos constitutos esse peccatores: quod indicat, in illis, qui nascuntur ex Adamo, esse vitium, propter quod peccatores dici possint. Sed hoc putat Pighius se posse eludere, quod peccatores interdum dicantur propter reatum, quamvis actio peccandi praeterierit, neque amplius extet. Quamvis hoc ita sit, nunquam tamen ostendere potest e Scripturis, quenquam peccatorem appellari, quin aut in seipso vitium habeat, aut certe antea admiserit: nisi dicere velit, Deum homines reos facere absque ipsorum aliquo peccato. Num quid flagitare disertius tua potest, Lector, aequitas? Sed redeamus ad Argumentum nobis objectum. Quamvis causae nostrae non obsit conclusio, tamen Minor distingui debet. Nam si vult nos privari justitia naturali propter primam Adae inobedientiam nobis imputatam, petitio est, ut loquuntur, principii: id ipsum enim assumit quod versatur in quaestione: quare negatur minor. Sin vult nos privari justitia propter inobedientiam illam in nos, (non quidem secundum actum, sed secundum habitum) naturaliter propagatam, concedi potest. Nam inobedientia actualis Adamum justitia privavit, quam amissam cum posteris communicare non potuit: Nemo enim dat quod non habet. Negamus igitur nos privari justitia naturali ob peccatum Adami nobis imputatum: Concedimus nos ea privari ob peccatum Adami in nos propagatum.
latin.109: Instat D. Garissolius. Quid dico instat? Respondeo, inquit, nempe responsioni responsionem opponit. Sed quid tamen respondet? Resp. inquit, 1. Non si propagatio peccati & ejus transmissio per generationem naturalem concedenda est, ut est certissima, propterea imputationem negari, aut tolli consentaneum est; neque enim ab illius positione ad hujus negationem consequentia ulla legitima duci potest, utraque potius in causa peccati originalis conjungenda est, sicut a nostris Theologis communiter observari certum est. Atqui, inquam, nostrae, nunc quidem, partes sunt respondere, ejus probare. Ponimus autem, id quod est in confesso, propagari peccatum Adami per generationem naturalem. An eam antecedat imputatio peccati Adamici, necne, id ipsum est quod inter nos controversitur, quodque probandum suscepisse videbatur. Nunc probationis loco contentus est dicere ab illius positione ad hujus negationem nullam esse consequentiam. Fac ita esse, an propterea imputationem illam astruxit? probet igitur non sufficere propagationem naturalem, nisi eam antecedat imputatio, alioquin aerem diverberat. Atque hoc est quod intendit probare.
latin.110: Addit enim. 2. Nec satis est, si dicas Adamum, quae amiserat communicare non potuisse, eo quod nemo dat, quod non habet, quia hic ratio reddenda est, quare anima Adami justitiae originalis decoramentis ornata fuerit; & quare posterorum ipsius animae, quae non traducuntur propagatione naturali, sed a Deo infundendo creantur, & creando infunduntur, iisdem ornatibus ipsa sua creatione careant, adeoque perfectione illa prima patris Adami destitutae in corpus a Deo inducantur, quod tamen aliter futurum fuit, si Adam in integritate sua perstitisset. Hic enim non est simpliciter recurrendum ad propagationem, cum animae non propagentur, aut traducantur; Neque ad legem naturae, qua morbosi morbosos generant, quia anima non generatur, & tamen ab initio sui esse, privata est primis illis beneficiis. 3. Quia non bene comparatur qualitas physica in carne sola haerens, qualis est morbus aut lepra, cum qualitate morali, qualis est corruptio sive peccatum originale. Neque sequitur, si vere naturale est, ut leprosus leprosum, aut elephantiacus elephantiacum generet, ut putandum sit a sola natura propagationis esse, citra omnem respectum imputationis, quod ex Adam moraliter corrupto generantur homines moraliter itidem corrupti. Primum quod ait, rationem reddendam esse quare anima Adami justitiae originalis decoramentis ornata fuerit, ea ratio est in promptu: cum enim rationalis & capax justitiae esset, creari a Deo optimo expers justitiae & sanctitatis, hoc est, injusta & immunda non potuit. Sed quare posterorum ejus animae eadem justitia, cum producuntur non ornantur? etiam obvia est responsio, quia immundus Adamus mundum generare non potuit: genuit enim sibi similes. Quid opus est, ut tibi ratione reddam, quare lupus lupum gignit? ut enim, inquit Gualterus, lupi lupos generant, ita Adam peccator peccatores genuit: & ut luporum catuli lupinam ingluviem non obscuris argumentis produnt, ita in infantibus quoque peccatum tunc quoque vires suas exerit, quando per aetatem opus adhuc nullum possunt perficere. At inquis, Hic non est simpliciter recurrendum ad propagationem, cum animae non propagentur aut traducantur. Ego vero publicae nostrae confessionis fidei non sum immemor. Art. 10. Nec putamus necessarium esse inquirere, quinam peccatum possit ab uno ad alterum propagari. Praeclara sunt etiam Petri Martyris, ut alios omittam, haec verba. Res quidem, inquit, obscura est, & perdifficilis: eoque minus arbitror de ea esse laborandum. Nam cum peccatum ipsum originis extare, & ad posteros transmitti, verbum Dei luculentissime doceat, quamvis modum, & rationem, qua transferatur non intelligamus, tamen veritati cedendum est: de modo autem qui difficulter sciri, & sine jactura ignorari potest, non nimis sollicite, atque anxie disputandum. Re vera constat, multa esse, quae, quomodo producta fuerint, ignoramus. Praestat modesta ignorantia audaci & incertae scientiae. Sed quoniam nobis per Viri docti ratiocinationem non licet ita sobrie sapere, Peto, an peccatum haereditarium propagetur naturaliter, nec-ne? Propagatur, inquit, quia mundum ex immundo nemo elicere potest, quia corruptus Adam corruptos genuit, quia Deus permisit labem illam a primis parentibus peccato contractam haerere in semine, & ad posteros promanare. Ita est, neque aliquis nostrum erit, qui non totum illud prolixissime largiatur. Hoc sane verissimum est, & adversus Pelagianos ab omnibus orthodoxis constanter assertum.
latin.111: Considera ergo, Lector, quid possis respondere has ipsas D. Garissolii, quibus nos oppugnat, rationes, in illam propagationem retorquenti. Quomodo propagatur peccatum haereditarium, cum animae, quibus inhaeret, non propagentur, aut traducantur? Non potes confugere ad legem naturae, qua morbosi morbosos generant, quia anima non generatur, & tamen ab initio sui esse privata est justitia & corrupta. Quomodo etiam potest labes illa, cum non sit qualitas physica, sed moralis haerere in semine? Aut ego vehementer fallor, aut non poteris his rationibus, quatenus simpliciter propagationem peccati impugnant, occurrere, quin eadem opera nos ab eis praestes immunes. Nam si recurras ad imputationem, nihil proficies. Imputatio enim est actio non hominis generantis, sed Dei judicantis. Deinde, vult D. Garissolius imputationem illam tunc fuisse factam, cum primum peccavit Adamus, diu antequam propagatio seu generatio fieret: ut quomodo propagationis naturalis pars aliqua dici possit, haud equidem intelligam. Quod si per imputationem poenae irrogationem ob Adami peccatum intelligis, illa ipsa irrogatio Dei actio est, non autem naturae aut hominis gignentis. Deinde illa poena, quae eadem peccatum est, vel producitur a gignente, vel non. Si producitur, redeunt superiores rationes, quomodo enim potest ab homine gignente produci peccatum in anima quae ab eo non gignitur? Si non producitur, certe non propagatur. Vides ergo a D. Garissolio propagationis peccati nomen retineri, rem vero significatam tolli. Cum igitur in confesso sit, peccatum per generationem carnalem propagari, juxta illud quod ex carne natum est, caro est; Et rationes illae a Pelagianis adversus orthodoxos centies sint objectae, nihil opus est ut iis solvendis remoremur lectorem. Consulti possunt Augustinus, Martyr, Chamierus, aliique plurimi, qui de propagatione peccati diligenter scripserunt. Sic se habuit prima D. Garissolii ratio.

pass_a.106: Chapter heading: Caput X — the claim that antecedent / immediate imputation of Adam's first actual sin can be built up by reasons is false; no reasons can establish it. Address to the reader: given that this imputation is missing from Scripture, can reasons still build it? Placeus will hear the reasons offered anyway. Standing conviction: sound reason never parts company with Scripture. Concession: God's gifts to Adam were not for Adam alone but for the whole line after him; spoiled of those goods in Adam's person, we fell into the full misery and curse. From that concession, though, no argument for the disputed imputation follows. Question 1: were Adam's bestowed goods themselves to be charged to every descendant by imputation? Question 2: is the matching stripping of those goods to be charged to us by imputation? Wish: if only that stripping touched us merely by way of imputation!
pass_a.107: Opponent's major: children stripped of benefits their parents had taken for self and offspring because of some actual parental crime — those children pay the father's-crime penalties, and therefore the father's crime is imputed to them. Minor applied to Adam: every natural descendant, for that first polluting disobedience, loses the natural justice and uprightness Adam had received for himself and his line. Conclusion drawn: every natural descendant pays those paternal-crime penalties, so the crime is imputed. Placeus's fork if the conclusion is granted: take 'paternal crime' as the hereditary vice itself → then yes imputed, and immediately; take it as the cause of that vice (Adam's actual disobedience) → also imputed, but only through the inherent vice as means. Penalty timing: we pay nearby for the sin propagated into us, farther back for Adam's old act. Bare-immediate reading rejected: anyone who says we are born liable to Adam's trespass with no vice, fault, or depravity in us is repeating Pighius; Martyr explained and chiefly overthrew that error — reader, weigh whether those same blows hit Garissoles's thesis.
pass_a.108: Martyr's first blow at Pighius: infants die; death has no claim where sin is absent unless God punishes the guiltless. Paul used death's reign from Adam to Moses to prove sin before the Law. Under Pighius that proof goes soft — death blamed on Adam while denying they had sin. Placeus's read of Martyr: the 'sin' in view is our habitual corruption, not Adam's bare act the way Garissoles wants; so Martyr's case against Pighius also cuts against Garissoles. Second Martyr blow: by one man's disobedience many were set down as sinners — that marks a vice in Adam's offspring by which the name 'sinner' fits. Pighius's dodge (sinner by leftover guilt after the act is gone) never finds in Scripture a 'sinner' lacking either present vice or a prior deed — unless God invents guilt with no sin of theirs. Back to the objected syllogism: the conclusion need not hurt Placeus, but the minor must be split. Reading A — deprived of natural justice because Adam's first disobedience is imputed: that steals the question; deny the minor. Reading B — deprived because that disobedience (as habit, not as act) is naturally propagated into us: grantable. Actual disobedience emptied Adam of justice he could not hand on — nobody gives what he lacks. Verdict line: deny privation by imputed Adam-sin; grant privation by Adam-sin propagated into us.
pass_a.109: Garissoles 'presses' — better: he answers an answer. His Reply 1: even when sin's natural-generation transmission is granted as rock-certain, that grant does not license denying or canceling imputation; you cannot validly go from affirming propagation to denying imputation; both belong together in original sin's cause, as our theologians usually note. Placeus's role split: we answer; he must prove. Agreed premise: Adam's sin travels by natural generation. Open question he looked ready to prove: does an Adamite-sin imputation come first? What he offers instead of proof: there is no logical leap from affirming propagation to denying imputation. Even if that is so — has he thereby built the imputation? He must show natural propagation is insufficient unless imputation precedes it; if not, he is striking air. That insufficiency claim is exactly what he means to prove next.
pass_a.110: Garissoles Reply 2 stretches beyond 'no one gives what he lacks.' He demands a reason why Adam's soul wore original-justice ornaments, while later souls — not carried along by natural traduction but created when God infuses them — lack those same ornaments from the moment of creation and are led into the body missing the father's first perfection; that lack, he adds, would not have been so if Adam had stayed whole. He forbids a simple appeal to propagation, because souls are not propagated or traduced. He also forbids appeal to nature's rule that the diseased generate the diseased, because the soul is not generated, and yet from the first instant of its being it is stripped of those first benefits. Reply 3: a physical quality that sticks only in flesh (disease, leprosy) is a poor twin for a moral quality such as corruption or original sin. Even if a leper naturally generates a leper, or an elephantiac an elephantiac, it does not follow that moral corruption descending from morally corrupt Adam is from propagation's nature alone, with no regard whatever to imputation. Placeus answers the adornment question at once: a rational soul able to hold justice could not be made by the best God empty of justice and holiness — that is, unjust and unclean. Why posterity's souls are not so adorned when produced? Because unclean Adam could not father a clean child; he begot his like. Why a wolf begets a wolf needs no deep theory; Gualther: wolves generate wolves, so sinner Adam generated sinners; wolf-cubs show wolfish greed by clear marks, and in infants sin likewise puts out its strength before age lets them finish any work. Against the 'souls are not propagated' push: Placeus remembers the public confession, Article 10 — it is not necessary to settle how sin can pass from one to another. Martyr too: the mode is obscure and very hard, so less toil should go there; Scripture teaches most clearly that original sin exists and is transmitted; yield to that truth even when the transfer mode is unknown; do not dispute anxiously what is hard to know and safe to leave unknown. Modest ignorance outranks bold uncertain knowledge. Still, Garissoles's reasoning will not let Placeus rest sober, so he asks point-blank: is hereditary sin naturally propagated or not? Garissoles says yes — clean cannot be drawn from unclean; corrupt Adam begot corrupt; God allowed the blot contracted by the first parents' sin to cling in the seed and flow to posterity. Placeus: so it is; none of us refuse that grant at length; it is most true and the constant orthodox answer against the Pelagians.
pass_a.111: Retorsion: take Garissoles's own anti-propagation reasons and aim them at the propagation he still names. How does hereditary sin propagate if the souls it sticks in are not propagated? Nature's diseased→diseased law fails: the soul is not generated, yet from the start it is justice-stripped and corrupt. How does a moral (not physical) blot lodge in seed? Either Placeus is badly wrong, or those reasons — insofar as they attack bare propagation — also clear Placeus unless Garissoles softens them. Fleeing to imputation does not help: imputation is God's judging act, not the begetter's generating act. Timing problem: Garissoles sets the imputation at Adam's first sin, long before generation — so it is hard to call it a piece of natural propagation. If 'imputation' means penalty inflicted for Adam's sin, that infliction is God's act, not nature's or the father's. Penalty/sin either is produced by the begetter or is not. Produced → earlier puzzles return (how produce sin in a soul he does not beget?). Not produced → not propagated. Result: Garissoles keeps the word 'propagation' and drops the thing. Since carnal propagation of sin is confessed (what is born of flesh is flesh), and Pelagians have thrown these objections a hundred times, no need to hold the reader on solving them — see Augustine, Martyr, Chamier, and others. End of Garissoles's first reason; the second (alteram) is not opened here.

106:
Chapter X. That the antecedent or immediate imputation of Adam's first actual sin cannot be established by any reasons.

Do you think, reader, that this imputation — since it is absent from Scripture — can be established by reasons? Still, let us hear whatever reasons are brought forward. For we are persuaded that right reason always agrees with Scripture. I grant that what God had bestowed on Adam was given not to him alone but also to his whole posterity; and therefore that we, spoiled of all those goods in his person, fell into this whole misery and curse. What reason for that imputation can be drawn from that? Were all the goods God had bestowed on Adam to be imputed to every one of his posterity? Or is the fitting spoliation of all those goods to be imputed to us? Would that this spoliation belonged to us only by imputation!
107: Whoever, he says, are deprived of those benefits which those parents had received both for themselves and for their children because of some actual crime of the parents — those people suffer the penalties of the father's crime, and so the father's crime is imputed to them. But all Adam's posterity, because of that first disobedience of his by which he polluted himself, are deprived of those benefits which Adam had received for himself and for his posterity — namely, natural justice and uprightness. Therefore all Adam's natural posterity suffer the penalties of the father's crime, and so that paternal crime is imputed to them. What if I grant this conclusion? For paternal crime is understood either as the hereditary vice, or as the cause of that vice — Adam's actual disobedience. If the former, it is imputed, and indeed immediately. If the latter, that too is imputed, but by means of the inherent vice. We suffer the penalties proximately for our own sin propagated into us, and remotely for the sin once committed by Adam. But if someone says that we are all born liable to Adam's transgression immediately — that is, not because of any vice or fault or depravity that we have in ourselves — let him remember that this was Pighius's error as Peter Martyr explained it, and as it was chiefly confuted by these arguments. Consider them, reader, if you please, and whether they do not fight against D. Garissoles's sentence and arguments.
108: But, he says, against this sentence that chiefly tells which we have already said twice: namely, that infants die. For death has no right where there is no sin — unless we would say that God punishes an innocent person. And this reason is confirmed from Paul's argument by which he proved that sin was before the Law: Because death, he says, reigned from Adam until Moses. Yet on Pighius's sentence this reason might seem dullest of all. For someone would say that even if those people died, it still does not follow from that that they had sin. For death came upon them because of Adam, on account of whose sin they were made mortal. You see, reader, that the sin understood is not Adam's actual sin, as D. Garissoles wants, but our habitual sin; and that his arguments fight for Pighius's cause against ours. To make that plainer, I will add another argument of Martyr's. Finally, he says, we have from Paul that by one man's disobedience many were constituted sinners: which indicates that in those who are born of Adam there is a vice because of which they can be called sinners. But Pighius thinks he can evade this, because sinners are sometimes so called because of guilt, even though the act of sinning has passed and no longer exists. Though that is so, he can never show from the Scriptures that anyone is called a sinner unless he either has a vice in himself or has certainly committed one before — unless he would say that God makes people guilty without any sin of theirs. Can your fairness, reader, ask anything more plainly? But let us return to the argument objected against us. Although the conclusion does not hinder our cause, still the minor must be distinguished. For if he wants us deprived of natural justice because of Adam's first disobedience imputed to us, that is begging the question, as they say: for it assumes the very point under dispute; and so the minor is denied. But if he wants us deprived of justice because of that disobedience naturally propagated into us (not indeed according to the act, but according to the habit), that can be granted. For actual disobedience stripped Adam of justice, and once he had lost it he could not communicate it to his posterity: for no one gives what he does not have. We therefore deny that we are deprived of natural justice because of Adam's sin imputed to us; we concede that we are deprived of it because of Adam's sin propagated into us.
109: D. Garissoles presses on. Why do I say presses on? I answer, he says — that is, he sets a reply against a reply. But what does he answer? Reply, he says, 1. Even if the propagation of sin and its transmission by natural generation is to be granted, as it most certainly is, it is not therefore fitting that imputation be denied or removed; nor can any legitimate consequence be drawn from affirming the one to denying the other. Rather both are to be joined in the cause of original sin, as it is certain our theologians commonly observe. But I say: our part now is to answer, his to prove. And we lay down what is confessed: that Adam's sin is propagated by natural generation. Whether an imputation of Adamite sin precedes that propagation or not — that itself is what is in controversy between us, and what he seemed to have undertaken to prove. Now, in place of proof, he is content to say that from affirming the one there is no consequence to denying the other. Grant that it is so: has he thereby established that imputation? Let him therefore prove that natural propagation is not enough unless imputation precedes it; otherwise he is beating the air. And that is what he means to prove.
110: For he adds: 2. Nor is it enough if you say that Adam could not communicate what he had lost, because no one gives what he does not have — because here a reason must be given why Adam's soul was adorned with the ornaments of original justice; and why the souls of his posterity, which are not traduced by natural propagation but are created by God in infusion and infused in creation, lack those same ornaments from their very creation, and so are brought by God into the body destitute of that first perfection of father Adam — which would nevertheless have been otherwise if Adam had persisted in his integrity. For here one must not simply recur to propagation, since souls are not propagated or traduced; nor to the law of nature by which the diseased generate the diseased, because the soul is not generated, and yet from the beginning of its being it is deprived of those first benefits. 3. Because a physical quality inhering in flesh alone, such as disease or leprosy, is not well compared with a moral quality such as corruption or original sin. Nor does it follow that if it is truly natural for a leper to generate a leper, or an elephantiac an elephantiac, one should think it is from the nature of propagation alone, apart from every respect to imputation, that from morally corrupt Adam morally corrupt people likewise are generated. First, as for what he says — that a reason must be given why Adam's soul was adorned with the ornaments of original justice — that reason is ready to hand: for since it was rational and capable of justice, it could not be created by the best God without justice and holiness — that is, unjust and unclean. But why are the souls of his posterity not adorned with the same justice when they are produced? The answer is ready too: because unclean Adam could not generate a clean one; for he begot like himself. What need is there for me to give you a reason why a wolf begets a wolf? For as Gualther says, as wolves generate wolves, so Adam the sinner generated sinners; and as wolf cubs show wolfish greed by no obscure proofs, so in infants also sin then exerts its forces when by age they can yet perform no work. But you say: here one must not simply recur to propagation, since souls are not propagated or traduced. I for my part am not forgetful of our public confession of faith. Article 10: Nor do we think it necessary to inquire how sin can be propagated from one to another. Peter Martyr's words too are excellent, to omit others: The matter, he says, is obscure and very hard; and for that reason I think less labor should be spent on it. For since the word of God most clearly teaches that original sin itself exists and is transmitted to posterity, although we do not understand the mode and reason by which it is transferred, still we must yield to the truth; but on a mode that can be known only with difficulty and ignored without loss, one should not dispute too anxiously. In truth it is clear that there are many things whose manner of production we do not know. Modest ignorance is better than bold and uncertain knowledge. But since the learned man's reasoning will not let us be so sober, I ask: is hereditary sin propagated naturally, or not? It is propagated, he says, because no one can draw what is clean from what is unclean, because corrupt Adam begot corrupt people, because God permitted that blot contracted by the first parents' sin to cling in the seed and flow out to posterity. So it is; and there will be none of us who will not grant all that at great length. That is most true, and constantly asserted by all the orthodox against the Pelagians.
111: Consider then, reader, what you can answer when those very reasons of D. Garissoles by which he attacks us are turned back against that propagation. How is hereditary sin propagated, when the souls in which it inheres are not propagated or traduced? You cannot flee to the law of nature by which the diseased generate the diseased, because the soul is not generated, and yet from the beginning of its being it is deprived of justice and corrupted. How also can that blot cling in the seed, when it is not a physical quality but a moral one? Either I am badly mistaken, or you will not be able to meet those reasons insofar as they simply attack the propagation of sin without by the same stroke leaving us immune from them. For if you recur to imputation, you will gain nothing. For imputation is an action not of the generating man but of God judging. Further, D. Garissoles wants that imputation to have been done when Adam first sinned, long before propagation or generation took place — so how it can be called any part of natural propagation I for my part do not understand. But if by imputation you mean the infliction of a penalty for Adam's sin, that infliction itself is God's action, not nature's or the begetting man's. Then that penalty, which is also sin, is either produced by the begetter or not. If it is produced, the earlier reasons return: for how can sin be produced by the begetting man in a soul that is not begotten by him? If it is not produced, certainly it is not propagated. So you see that by D. Garissoles the name of sin's propagation is kept, but the thing signified is taken away. Since therefore it is confessed that sin is propagated by carnal generation, according to that saying what is born of the flesh is flesh; and those reasons have been objected a hundred times by the Pelagians against the orthodox, there is no need for us to detain the reader in solving them. Augustine, Martyr, Chamier, and many others who have written carefully on the propagation of sin may be consulted. So stood D. Garissoles's first reason.

Minor beg if imputed; concede habitual propagation; deny imputed / concede propagated.

111: Retorsion: Garissoles's anti-propagation reasons rebound; imputation is God's judging, not generating.
First Garissoles ratio closed; stops before Adjungo alteram.
